zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Consulted after independent scan reading; the returned transcription and notes are reviewer-authored, not a reproduction of the index.

runs.text: arſe facilmente à virtude, ou ſer leuado facil-

lines.note: Continues a verb from the preceding page: readily turning to virtue, or being led by it. The opening arſe is partly obscured by heavy ink; it is retained as a divided continuation, not expanded into a conjectural whole verb.
Completes facil-mente and the description of being easily led by virtue. This short continuation belongs to the preceding entry.
Zenyuu is explained by yoki tomo, good companions; the Portuguese offers good companions or good company. The caron over u and abbreviation tilde in Bõs are distinct marks.
Companhia completes boa companhia, the collective alternative to individual good companions.
Zenzai is here good treasure or wealth, as yoki takara and boas riquezas both indicate. It is distinct from the exclamation in the following entry.
Completes the alternative gloss as a good and valuable thing; rica qualifies couſa, rather than beginning a new definition.

This zenzai is an approving exclamation, yoki kana, translated as an exclamation over something good. The scan and aligned OCR read Ycqi, although the sense calls for yoki. This apparent c may be a damaged o; the anomalous printed-looking form is retained rather than silently repaired. S. is the upright written-register label.
Zenzoo is a monk of the Zen school, explicitly identified by Zen-shuu no soo. Bon- begins Portuguese Bonzo on the next row; the printed vowel marks are not standardized to one shape.

Completes Bonzo and specifies the Zen sect. Ienxùs is the sect-name embedded in the Portuguese explanation, with a Portuguese plural ending; enlargement supports a grave over u here, unlike the caron in the preceding roman example.
Zessoo is explained literally as the tongue's form and glossed simply as tongue. The printed mixed long and short s pair in Ieſsǒ is retained; S. is an upright register label.
Zet is the Sino-Japanese tongue element, matched to shita and Portuguese lingua. Its final t is preserved rather than expanded to a modern open syllable.

runs.text: Certo lugar dos pees onde ſe dão botões

lines.note: Zekkot denotes a particular site at the feet where cautery is applied. The Portuguese visibly has pees, not the OCR's pes; the definition describes the historical treatment rather than giving advice.
De fogo completes botões de fogo, the cautery expression explaining the site named in the preceding row.
Zetgaku means abandoning or interrupting study. This first explanation is followed by a more specific sense concerning completed learning.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Deixar de eſtudar depois de ſe con-

lines.note: The second sense is ceasing to study after becoming accomplished; con- continues as ſumar below. The paragraph mark introduces another sense of the same headword.
Completes con-ſumar: attaining accomplishment in study or letters before stopping. The scan supports m in ſumar and t in letras, correcting the OCR's ſunar and leiras.

runs.text: Ietguen. Cotobauo tayaſu. i, Gongo dǒdã.

lines.note: Zetgen is explained as cutting off words and as gongo doodan, the exhaustion of verbal expression. The initial of Gongo is G, not OCR C; the final nasal remains abbreviated by the tilde.

runs.text: O não poder explicar com palauras. S.

lines.note: The gloss specifies inability to explain in words, establishing the intended sense of the Japanese expressions above. S. remains outside the italic prose.

Zetmet, with tae horoburu, means complete extinction or destruction. Enlargement supports foroburu, not OCR fotoburu. The damaged Portuguese word is read as Deſtruição in agreement with total and the Japanese; the upright S. marks written usage.

runs.text: Couſa marauilhoſa, & que não ſe po-

lines.note: Zetmyoo here denotes something wonderful beyond verbal explanation. Its circumflex distinguishes the printed headword from the caroned form in the next entry.
Completes po-de and the claim that the wonderful thing cannot be expressed in words.
The distinct caroned zetmyoo is glossed as the beginning of destruction. Co- begins the demonstrative cono in the example below, not a Portuguese word.

runs.text: no vazauaiua cano fitono tameni jetmiǒ-

lines.note: With Co- above, the example says that this calamity is a beginning of ruin for that person. The caron in jetmiǒ- agrees with this entry, not the previous wonderful-thing sense.

runs.text: Eſte trabalho he principio da perdição

lines.note: Già completes the Japanese assertion; the Portuguese calls the trouble the beginning of the person's ruin. The small i and the accent over a support già rather than OCR gùa.
Specifies whose ruin is meant: that man's. This completes the example from the preceding three physical lines.

Zetnai is pronunciation; the example begins with someone whose pronunciation is poor. The headword has n, matching Ietnaino, and the Portuguese noun has its final o. The subsequently consulted supplied NINJAL index likewise identifies Ietnai.
Hito completes the poor-pronunciation alternative; yoi hito ja supplies the good-pronunciation alternative. The tightly printed Hehomem is retained rather than silently respaced.
Completes the Portuguese contrast between bad and good pronunciation; boa coordinates with mà on the preceding row.

runs.text: Iet ri. Taye fanaruru. i, Gongono tayetaru

lines.note: Zetri is explained through separation or cessation, specifically the exhaustion of words. The visible internal space in Iet ri is retained without treating ri as an independent entry.

runs.text: Falta de palauras, como pera explicar

lines.note: Coto closes the Japanese explanatory phrase. The Portuguese defines a lack of words, for example when trying to explain something.
Completes the explanatory example with some thing that cannot be put into words. The tilde is retained over u in algũa.
Zetrin means something outstanding, matching sugureta koto and excellent thing. The headword's visible internal spacing is preserved.
Zetryoo denotes something beyond mental reach, as kokoro ni mo oyobanu states. The damaged capital is I, not OCR B; the spaced headword and caron are preserved.

runs.text: ſa que não ſe alcança com o entendimento. Vt,

lines.note: Completes Cou-ſa and explains that the understanding cannot reach it. Vt introduces the combined verbal-and-mental example below.
The example combines zetgen with zetryoo: neither expressible in words nor mentally comprehensible. The unaccented jetrionari is retained as printed rather than regularized to the headword's mark.

runs.text: com palauras, nẽ alcançar com o entendimẽto.

lines.note: Completes the paired limitations: not explainable in words and not graspable by the understanding. Both nẽ and entendimẽto preserve abbreviation tildes.

runs.text: Iettǒ. Taye tauoruru. i, Cuzzure fateta co

lines.note: Zettoo is glossed as complete collapse, with kuzure hateta koto divided across the row boundary. There is no supplied hyphen after co: the right edge shows the divided syllable without one.
To completes coto, and the Portuguese describes a thing completely destroyed. The existing short-s st transcription is retained pending the project's separate ligature audit.
The circumflexed zettoo is the tip of the tongue, explicitly shita no saki. Its mark and meaning distinguish it from the preceding destruction entry.
The example describes something that cannot be uttered with the tongue. Portuguese q̃ is an abbreviated que and is not expanded in the transcription.

runs.text: não ſe pode explicar com palauras. S.

lines.note: Completes the translation as something that cannot be explained in words. The written-register S. is upright, not part of the italic sentence.
Zet-on concerns the voice of speakers, explained by shita and koe. The printed space in Iet von is retained rather than joining the headword editorially.
Zetshi, zetsuru means cutting off or interrupting, compared with tayuru and tatsu. The abbreviated principal form ſuru is not a separate Portuguese word.
Completes the interruption gloss and introduces shoshin wo zetsuru, breaking off correspondence. Ha begins the Portuguese explanation of a long lapse in writing.

runs.text: muito tempo que não vos viſito por carta.

lines.note: Explains the example pragmatically: it has been a long time since writing to the addressee. Viſito por carta means a visit by letter, not a physical visit.
The visible paragraph mark introduces gongo wo zetsuru, ceasing speech. It was omitted by the OCR; the alternative explanation continues on the next row.

runs.text: não poder falar, & de clarar algũa couſa.

lines.note: The second explanation is inability to speak or explain something. The printed internal gap in de clarar is retained rather than silently modernizing the spacing.

runs.text: Iexxe. Yo tayuru. i, Yoni ſugururu coto.

lines.note: Zesse is explained as surpassing the world or ages, with yo ni sugururu koto clarifying excellence. Its Portuguese explanation follows on the next physical line.

runs.text: Couſa excellente, ou q̃ excede as idades paſſadas.

lines.note: The gloss describes something excellent or surpassing past ages. Idades has a, not the OCR's o; q̃ remains an abbreviation. This is an indented continuation, despite the draft's unindented placement.
Zesshin combines tongue and lips, explicitly shita and kuchibiru. The first character matches the column's I types, not OCR A.
Zesshiki is the sense of taste. The existing short-s st reading in gosto is retained without imposing a global ligature classification.
Zesshoo is something excellent beyond adequate utterance, explained by tonaye tayuru. The period after excellente is retained even though the prose continues below.

runs.text: ou marauilhoſa, & que não ſe pode explicar

lines.note: Adds the alternative wonderful and states that words cannot explain it. Marauilhoſa is one printed word; the OCR's internal space is spurious. The row is an indented continuation.
The example begins kimyoo zesshoo no itari, an extreme of wondrous inexpressibility. The circumflex in Qimeô and caron in jexxǒno remain distinct.
Nari closes the Japanese assertion, translated as a wonderful thing. S. is the upright written-register label.

runs.text: Iexxǒ. Tamazzuſa tayuru. i, Fumiuo fiſa-

lines.note: This different zesshoo concerns a lapse in correspondence. The explanatory fumi wo hisa- continues into xǔ below; the damaged first consonant is read as f, not OCR ſ, in the sense of a long interval.
Completes fiſa-xǔ cacanu, not writing a letter for a long time. The caron over u is kept rather than modernizing the historical adverbial form.
Tempo completes the duration gloss; the upright S. marks this use as written language. The following display heading starts a new alphabetical subsection.

runs.text: Varela, ou moſteiro. Mas naõſe vſa

lines.note: Ji here means a temple or monastery. The large initial I and the following capital I together form printed II.; the OCR omitted the second character. The statement about use only in compounds continues below.
The temple element occurs in compounds, illustrated by jichuu and jinai. The tilde over the final o of compoſiçaõ is retained, independently of algũa's u-tilde.
Jiryoo, temple land or holdings, is the third compound illustrating the temple element. It is a short continuation, not a separate entry.

runs.text: Hora: não ſe vſa ſem algũa compo-

lines.note: Ji here is time, corresponding to toki and hora. The initial is capital I followed by lowercase i; the restriction to compounds continues below.
Completes compo-ſição and illustrates jiji kokkoku ni, at every hour or moment. The Portuguese gives each hour and a broader alternative below.
Completes the translation as at all times. It belongs to the repeated time-expression, not the following refusal entry.
Ji here is refusal or resistance, identified with jitai. The example begins gyoi wo, a superior's will or command; the damaged headword initial is I, not OCR F.
Jisuru completes the example of resisting what one is ordered to do. The bilingual context confirms refusal rather than the adjacent time or letter senses of ji.
Ji here is a written character. Jiwake ga miyenu means the writing cannot be distinguished; the Portuguese has Letra, not OCR Leira.
Completes the translation: this character or handwriting cannot be read. The negative Não belongs to the preceding physical line.
Ji denotes a child, with chigo as the Japanese equivalent and minino in Portuguese. The following qualification concerns use in compounds.
Explains combination with other syllables or words, illustrated by jishi. The visible y in ſyllabas replaces OCR o; Iixi begins with capital I, not lowercase l.
The first Idem refers back to child; yeiji, explained as midoriko, supplies another infant term. Both Idem labels belong to the italic explanatory apparatus.
Ji here denotes warriors or soldiers, matched by tsuwamono. Guer- begins the Portuguese word for war, completed on the next row.
Completes guerra and illustrates taking valiant soldiers along. The printed Yumiǒ spelling and caron are retained; Le- begins leuar in the translation.
Completes Le-uar and specifies bringing brave soldiers with oneself. The initial in ſoldados is long s, not the OCR's f.
Ji is a matter or thing, matched to koto. The example ano hito ji ga naranu is explained idiomatically as lack of means rather than translated word for word.

runs.text: Aquelle homem he pobre, ou não tem

lines.note: Nu completes naranu; the Portuguese says that man is poor or lacks something, with the object supplied below.
Poſſe completes não tem poſſe: the man lacks resources or means. This one-word continuation is genuine body text.
Jiai is here love or care for oneself, explicitly mizukara aisuru. The Portuguese more generally says to cherish and show affection; that difference is not corrected editorially.
Completes mo-ſtrar amor, showing love. The separated A mimar in the preceding row is retained as printed rather than silently joined.
This jiai is tender, compassionate affection, distinguished by itsukushimi aisuru. The Portuguese describes cherishing with great affection and love; grã- continues below.
Completes grã-de and names affection and love as the qualities of this compassionate jiai.
Jian combines a temple with a hermitage, represented by tera and iwori; Portuguese ermida gives the small religious-retreat sense.
Jibaku means binding oneself, explicitly mizukara shibaru. The Portuguese continues into an explanation of voluntary restraint rather than literal bonds alone.

runs.text: marrarſe aßi meſmo com algũa ley, ou com a

lines.note: Completes a-marrarſe and describes binding oneself by a rule or law. The alternative means of self-restraint follows below; the spelling and spacing of aßi are preserved.
Mortificação completes the alternative as ascetic self-denial. This is the dictionary's historical religious explanation of self-binding.
Jibai means selling oneself, matching mizukara uru and venderſe. The worn middle consonant of vru is read as r rather than OCR i; initial v represents the vowel in this Japanese verb.
Completes meſ-mo and illustrates jibai jitoku: selling oneself and personally obtaining the proceeds. The second meſ- continues below.
Completes the example as benefiting oneself from the price. The scan supports aproueitarſe, correcting OCR aproueitatſe.

runs.text: Iibo. Itçucuximu faua. i, Iifino faua.

lines.note: Jibo is a loving or compassionate mother, explained by itsukushimu hawa and jihi no hawa. The historical faua is retained, not modernized to haha; Mãy begins the Portuguese noun phrase.
Describes the mother as compassionate or loving, completing Mãy above. The reading piadoſa follows the damaged but compatible letters, not a new lexical item.
Jiboku denotes ears and eyes, explicitly mimi and me. The example continues on the next page, whose initial Fito is anticipated by the separate catchword below; it is not added to this body line.
